opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key is that nobody in Picbreeder was actually trying to get anywhere in particular. That sounds like a weakness, but it turns out to be the secret ingredient.

Here's what happens. Someone starts with a blob or some random pattern, and they pick the one that looks interesting. Then someone else comes along later, branches off that, and picks what *they* find interesting. Over many generations and many people, you get these chains of stepping stones. And the remarkable thing is that the person who discovered, say, the skull image was not trying to get a skull. They might have been evolving something that looked like an alien face or a weird symmetric shape, and then suddenly the skull appeared, and they recognized it and said, "oh, that's cool."

So why does that lead to rich representations? When we went back and looked inside the networks, the CPPNs that encode these images, we found something kind of shocking. They're incredibly well organized. In the skull, there's effectively a parameter that makes the mouth open and close. In the apple, there's something that controls the stem swinging back and forth. The representation is factored in a way that mirrors the actual structure of the object. It's almost like the network "understands" what a skull is, in a loose sense.

Compare that to training a network with SGD to output the same skull image. You can get a pixel-perfect match, but inside it's a mess. It's what we've called fractured and entangled representation. The output is right, but the internal structure has none of that elegant decomposition. Perturb the weights and you just get garbage, not a skull with its mouth opening.

I think the reason for the difference comes down to the path. In Picbreeder, every stepping stone along the way was something a human found interesting on its own terms. Humans tend to latch onto things like symmetry, regularity, modularity. Those are deep principles of how the world is organized. So each step was selected because it embodied some kind of meaningful regularity, and those regularities got locked in and then elaborated upon. By the time you reach the skull, it's built on a foundation of well-organized building blocks, like symmetry first, then something face-like, then refinements on top.

Objective-driven optimization doesn't care about any of that. It just wants to reduce the error. So it'll take any shortcut and grab whatever weird combination of weights gets the pixels right, and you get this fractured structure underneath.

And this connects to the bigger theme I've been talking about for years with Joel Lehman in *Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned*: if you set an ambitious objective and push straight toward it, the objective itself can be deceptive. The stepping stones that lead to great things often don't resemble the final destination. Picbreeder is almost a laboratory demonstration of that. The only way people got to these images was by *not* trying to get to them.

I'd also say this has real implications for AI today. We're scaling up these massive models and they're doing amazing things, but if their internal representations are fractured and entangled, that might limit things like creativity, generalization, and continual learning, even when the benchmark performance looks great. Picbreeder hints that there may be a very different kind of representation possible, one you only get by following an open-ended, interestingness-driven path rather than a pure objective.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that really surprised us at the time, and I think it's still underappreciated. Picbreeder was this website where people could evolve images. You'd see a grid of pictures, you'd click on the ones you liked, and those would be the parents of the next generation. And then crucially, you could publish what you found, and someone else could pick it up and keep going from there. So it was this huge collaborative branching tree of exploration.

And what came out of it were these remarkable images. A skull, a butterfly, a car, a face. And people would look at them and say, well, that's nice, but it's not that impressive, it's just a picture of a skull. But the interesting thing wasn't the picture. It was the representation underneath it. These images were encoded by neural networks, CPPNs, compositional pattern producing networks, and when you looked inside them, they were astonishingly elegant. The skull had a network where there was essentially a single node that controlled whether the mouth was open or closed. The car had one that moved the wheels. Nobody designed that. Nobody was trying to get that. There was no objective that said "give me a disentangled representation of a skull."

So the question is how did that happen? And I think the key is that nobody was trying to get a skull either. The person who found the skull wasn't searching for a skull. They were on some branch where someone had been evolving something that looked kind of like an alien face, and they saw something that reminded them of a skull and they followed it. The whole process was built on people following their own interest, stepping stone to stepping stone, with no fixed destination.

And what that does is it means the representations that survive are the ones that are good at being modified. If you're at generation thousand and someone's going to click on your children because they like how they look, then the kind of structure that persists is structure where a small change in the genome produces a meaningful, coherent change in the image. Symmetry gets locked in early, because people like symmetric things, and once it's locked in, everything downstream inherits it for free. Then you get regularities layered on top of regularities. The network is essentially being selected for a kind of evolvability, for having good knobs, even though no one is explicitly selecting for that.

Contrast that with what happens if you set an objective. If you say, I want a skull, and you optimize for skull-likeness from scratch, you get garbage. We actually tried this. You take the exact same encoding, the exact same search space, and you run an objective-driven search toward the images Picbreeder found, and it fails. It can't get there. Because the path to the skull goes through things that don't look like skulls at all. The objective is actively deceptive. It pulls you toward things that superficially resemble the goal while destroying the structure you'd actually need.

So I think of Picbreeder as kind of an existence proof. It shows that open-ended, interest-driven search, with lots of divergent branching, can produce representations that are better in a deep sense than what optimization produces, and it does so without anyone understanding or intending the result. Which, honestly, is a somewhat uncomfortable message for a field that's built almost entirely around objectives and benchmarks. But I think it's one we need to take seriously.

astra-6.text:
Well, the interesting thing is that the people choosing the images don’t have to understand the representation at all. They just see something that catches their eye, select it, and look at variations. But underneath that process, evolution is changing a network that generates the image.

And that network represents the image in a very different way from a list of pixels. It takes coordinates as inputs and produces the color at those coordinates. So a single change in the network can affect many parts of the image in a coordinated way. You can get symmetry, repetition, and patterns at different scales. Those are things evolution can build on.

Then the human supplies this very open-ended signal: that looks interesting. And “interesting” can change as you go. You might be exploring something that looks like a face, and suddenly it suggests a butterfly. You follow that possibility instead. Somebody else can pick up your image and take it in another direction.

So the richness comes from this interaction between a representation that can express regularities and a process that lets people keep discovering new possibilities. Nobody has to specify all the features of the eventual image in advance. The intermediate discoveries become stepping stones—even when nobody could have predicted what they would lead to.

sol-6.1.text:
The surprising thing is that nobody has to specify what the representation should be. In Picbreeder, people just see images, pick ones they find interesting, and let those images produce variations. But underneath that process, we're evolving networks that encode images as functions of coordinates. So the representation can capture regularities like symmetry, repetition, and patterns at different scales, rather than treating every pixel independently.

When somebody selects an image, they're also selecting that underlying encoding, even though they never see it. And that encoding determines what kinds of variations become possible next. So over many generations, you can accumulate structure that supports increasingly interesting discoveries.

The other key is that people don't have to keep pursuing the same objective. You might see something that looks vaguely like a face, follow it for a while, and then discover something entirely different. Someone else can branch from your image and take it somewhere you never imagined. Those intermediate discoveries become stepping stones.

So the richness comes from the interaction between a representation that can express regularities and an open-ended process that preserves interesting things without requiring us to know in advance what they're going to become.
